title: External sorting and aggregation
lead: External merge sort, ordered index scans, external hashing and grouped aggregates.
goals: Sorting and two-way external merge sort
Multiway merge sort and index order

sections.title: Sorting and two-way external merge sort
sections.html:
Sorting supports ORDER BY, duplicate elimination, grouping and sort-merge joins. If a file exceeds available memory, an external algorithm must explicitly control page reads and writes.

Two-way external merge sort first reads, sorts and writes each individual page as a run. Each later pass merges pairs of sorted runs. One input buffer per run and one output buffer are sufficient for merging.

For N pages, this version takes 1 + ⌈log₂N⌉ passes. If each pass reads and writes all pages, its I/O cost is 2N times the pass count. This includes writing the sorted result; pipelining that result changes the accounting.

PDF pp. 1–10

sections.title: Multiway merge sort and index order
sections.html:
With B buffers, pass 0 produces ⌈N/B⌉ sorted runs. A merge pass combines up to B − 1 input runs, reserving one buffer for output. The pass count is 1 + ⌈logB−1⌈N/B⌉⌉ for a nonempty input, with one initial pass when everything fits.

The slide example has N = 108 and B = 5: 22 initial runs, then 6, then 2, then 1. Four passes cost 2·108·4 = 864 page I/Os.

A clustered B+ tree can supply records in key order without a separate external sort. Following an unclustered index in key order can instead fetch one data page per record, so it must be compared with scan-and-sort.

PDF pp. 11–17

sections.title: Duplicate elimination and external hashing
sections.html:
Sorting places equal values consecutively, so duplicate elimination can retain one tuple from each equal group. If ordering is unnecessary, hashing can group equal values without producing a global order.

External hashing partitions the input on disk with a hash function, using one input buffer and up to B − 1 output buffers. Every occurrence of a key goes to the same partition. Each partition is then processed using an in-memory hash table and a second hash function.

The hash table, rather than just the partition’s raw bytes, must fit memory. Oversized partitions require recursive partitioning or another strategy. Skew can prevent even partition sizes.

PDF pp. 18–28

sections.title: Hash aggregation and memory requirements
sections.html:
Hash aggregation stores a group key and running aggregate state. COUNT stores a count; SUM a sum; MIN/MAX the current extremum. AVG requires both sum and count, combined only when the group result is produced.

During partitioning, equal group keys must remain together. The rehash phase updates each group’s state rather than retaining every original tuple when the aggregate permits this. Partial aggregation can therefore reduce intermediate volume.

The source’s rough two-phase capacity is B(B − 1) pages under even distribution, adjusted for hash-table overhead by a factor f. Sorting is useful when ordered output is also needed; hashing is often preferred for unordered grouping and DISTINCT.

PDF pp. 29–32

quiz.question: For N=90 and B=6, how many I/Os does multiway sorting require when the final output is written?
quiz.explanation: Pass 0 reads and writes 90 pages and creates 15 runs. Five input frames plus one output frame merge them into 3 runs, then 1. These are three complete passes, each 90 reads+90 writes=180 I/Os: 3×180=540, including the final sorted-file write.
